chunks: Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan and 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father — both together — from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hisham ibn al-Hakam, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him)
regarding the words of God, Blessed and Exalted: 'or two others from among others than you'
He said: 'If the man was in a city in which there is no Muslim, the testimony of one who is not a Muslim upon the bequest is permissible.'

key_terms.الْوَصِيَّة: bequest or will — a legal document designating the disposal of one's property after death, governed by detailed rules in Islamic jurisprudence
key_terms.بَلَد: city or land — here indicating a region or locality where the traveller finds himself
key_terms.شَهَادَة: testimony or witnessing — a formal legal act required for the validity of many Islamic legal transactions including marriage, divorce, and bequest

ai.seo_question: Can a non-Muslim witness a bequest (wasiyya) in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) provides a jurisprudential interpretation of Quran 5:106, which permits non-Muslim witnesses for a bequest under exceptional circumstances. The ruling clarifies that when a Muslim finds himself in a land with no fellow Muslims and needs to establish a will or bequest, the testimony of non-Muslim witnesses is legally valid. This ruling reflects the Islamic principle of necessity (darura) adapted to situations where the normal requirement of Muslim witnesses cannot be met.
